title: A morning breath
tomorrow: two young monks ask an old abba how to pray always. his answer?

lines: A FULL MOON, A HALL OF ELDERS.
cards: Breathing courses love the word advanced. The Buddha did something stranger. In the Anapanasati Sutta it's the end of the rainy-season retreat at Savatthi, and the hall is full of monks, elders like Sariputta among them.
On the full-moon night the Buddha says he's so pleased with how they're practicing that he'll stay on another month.
When the next full moon comes, with the elders now teaching newer monks, he looks over the silent assembly and teaches breathing in and breathing out. Why?

teach.h: DON'T CHANGE THE BREATH. KNOW IT.
teach.b: The answer is in how he teaches it. He doesn't say breathe better.

teach.h: LONG AS LONG, SHORT AS SHORT.
teach.b: He says a monk goes to the forest, the root of a tree or an empty hut, sits with the body straight, and then: breathing in long, he knows he breathes in long. Breathing out short, he knows he breathes out short.
The work isn't changing the breath. It's knowing it while it happens.

teach.h: THE SAME BREATH LEADS ALL THE WAY.
teach.b: Then, step by step, the same breath carries more: calming the body, feeling joy, watching the mind, seeing that all of it changes. In the sutta this one practice, followed far enough, leads all the way to awakening.
That's the teaching, named plainly. Buddhists call it anapanasati, mindfulness of breathing in and out, and in the sutta it's both where the path starts and what the elders keep coming back to.
So the puzzle solves itself. The breath isn't the beginner's toy you outgrow.

It's the one object that is always here, at the root of a tree or at the edge of a bed, so the elders use it too. Sati, the Pali word in its name, means mindfulness: staying with what is happening while it happens.
And your phone is very good at pulling you somewhere else. Three breaths, known as breaths, is a small morning version of what the Buddha taught on that full-moon night.

how: Buddhist teachers in a number of schools teach anapanasati, mindfulness of breathing, asking students to know the breath rather than control it, as the Anapanasati Sutta describes.

o: a deep gulp of air to wake the body up fast
holding your breath while you check the news
breath you notice on purpose before the day grabs you

games.q: the Buddha's breath teaching: tap the pairs.
p: mindfulness of breathing in and out
he knows he breathes in long
when he taught it to the elders
one place the sutta says to sit

s: breath meditation is a beginner's exercise you outgrow
the Buddha taught it to an assembly full of senior monks, and said it leads all the way to awakening.
the sutta tells you to breathe slowly and deeply
it tells you to know the breath as it is: long as long, short as short.
in the sutta, the same breath leads on to calm, joy and seeing change
step by step, the breath carries the whole path of mindfulness.

games.q: your cousin wants to start meditating but calls breath-watching boring; she wants something advanced. what fits the Anapanasati Sutta?
o: known fully, the breath isn't a starter level; it's the whole path.
boring means it's working, so force each breath slower and deeper.
do breath for a week, then move on to something more advanced.
games.why: the Buddha taught breathing to his elders, not just to newcomers, and in the sutta the same breath leads to awakening.

practice: Sit up straight and let the breath come on its own. For each breath, know it the way the sutta says: breathing in long, I know it's long; breathing out short, I know it's short.
Don't fix anything, and when your mind drifts to the phone, come back to the very next breath.

wordCard.voice: A morning breath: the breath you already have, known as it comes and goes, before the day takes you. In the Buddha's teaching, anapanasati.

orig.note: Pali, the language of the Buddhist suttas (here in Devanagari): mindfulness of breathing in and out.

carryVoice: Your line: breath before phone. Three breaths, known as breaths, and then the screen. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 118, Anapanasati Sutta (the full-moon assembly at Savatthi; the elders; breathing in long, knowing it; the steps leading to awakening)
Digha Nikaya 22, Maha-Satipatthana Suttanta (the forest, the root of a tree, an empty place; mindfulness of breathing)
